bp: Scientific knowledge graphs are meant to turn research papers into facts that software can inspect. Instead of storing only a title, authors, and date, the Open Research Knowledge Graph records fine-grained triples: one piece names a thing, one piece names a relationship, and one piece names the thing on the other side. That middle relationship name, called a predicate or property, is small but decisive. If two contributors use different property names for the same relationship, machines see two separate facts where a human would see one idea. This matters for retrieval-augmented generation, where a language system is asked to answer from retrieved evidence instead of guessing. The graph can only ground an answer if its labels are stable enough to be searched, compared, and reused. This paper serves the plumbing layer of scientific AI: it cleans the shared vocabulary that makes structured research knowledge machine-actionable.
wh: The hard part is not that the graph lacks facts; it is that the fact language has been shaped by uncontrolled crowdsourcing. Many people can contribute useful structure, but they may choose different names, different spelling styles, or different levels of specificity for the same relation. One person may create a broad property, another may create a near synonym, and a third may choose a name whose intended meaning is unclear outside that local context. Machines do not gracefully infer that these are duplicates unless the schema tells them so. A retrieval system may miss evidence because it searches one property name but not its twin. A comparison tool may count two relations separately even though they should be merged. The tension is coverage versus order: crowdsourcing gives breadth, while machine-actionability requires a concise, consistent set of predicates with meanings that survive beyond the person who created them.
naive: A smart beginner might freeze the current ORKG property list and write a manual style guide for future contributors. That would prevent some new inconsistency, but it would not repair the existing duplicate and ambiguous properties already attached to data. Another beginner move is exact string cleanup: merge names that match after lowercasing, removing punctuation, or applying one naming convention. That catches surface mess, not meaning. Two properties can use different words and still describe the same relation; two similar-looking names can also mean different things. Pure manual cleanup has the opposite problem: experts can make good judgments, but reviewing a large property set one item at a time is slow and hard to keep consistent.
ap: The paper's central move is to treat ontology cleanup as a semi-automated consolidation task. A large language model, meaning a system trained to read and produce text, is used as a fast semantic sorter over the existing ORKG property set. It can propose which properties appear synonymous, redundant, ambiguously named, or inconsistent with a naming convention. Human ontology engineers then keep control over the final schema: they review, correct, and restructure the proposals instead of letting the model rewrite the scientific vocabulary alone. The output is OPO-Consolidated, a cleaned property ontology designed to reduce repeated meanings while preserving useful coverage. The approach is mechanical but not blind: use the model for broad language comparison, use human judgment for boundary cases, and evaluate the result against a gold standard dataset of 153 research papers.
mech: The input is the existing ORKG property ontology: many predicate names and their intended meanings as used in triples that describe scientific publications. The workflow first examines this property set for places where the same relationship has been named more than once, where naming conventions conflict, or where a property's meaning is too unclear to support automatic use. The language model supplies candidate refinements because it can compare phrases by ordinary meaning, not only by exact spelling. For example, it can flag that two differently worded labels may refer to the same kind of relation, while also noticing when a name does not follow a uniform pattern. Those suggestions become work items for human engineering. The human step decides which proposed merges are valid, which names should become canonical, and how the cleaned schema should be restructured so old data can still be understood. The transformation is therefore from a noisy crowd-built vocabulary to a consolidated schema. What comes out is not new paper content; it is a tighter map of allowed property meanings. The evaluation then checks the cleaned ontology on an established gold standard of 153 research papers, measuring whether the schema became more concise by resolving synonymy and redundancy and more semantically consistent through uniform naming.
math: The main mathematical idea is similarity as controlled comparison. Similarity here does not mean that two strings look alike; it means that two property descriptions point to the same relationship in the world of research papers. A model must compress words into comparable signals, then decide which differences matter. The tradeoff is compression versus detail: if the comparison is too loose, distinct scientific relations may be collapsed; if it is too strict, duplicate names remain. A second idea is clustering, the act of gathering items into groups because each group is believed to share one underlying meaning. Clustering is useful because redundancy is a group problem: the mistake is not one bad label, but several labels competing for the same role. A third idea is schema normalization, which is a rule-based form of consistency: choose one stable naming pattern so software can predict how relations are expressed. The human review adds a boundary condition to the math. The model can score and suggest semantic nearness, but ontology quality depends on expert decisions about whether two meanings are truly interchangeable. The paper's evaluation also uses measurement: conciseness asks whether fewer properties cover the same useful ground, while semantic consistency asks whether names obey a clearer shared logic.
dots: This paper sits in the knowledge graph curation theme because it works before downstream reasoning begins. Many graph papers in the repo ask how evidence should travel through connected facts; this one asks whether the labels on those connections are clean enough for evidence to travel at all. It is close to retrieval-augmented generation because the abstract says scientific knowledge graphs help ground generated answers and reduce unsupported claims. It is also a sibling of the LOPE property-extraction work noted elsewhere in the repo: LOPE focuses on extracting consistent properties from scientific papers, while this paper focuses on consolidating an existing crowdsourced property set. The recurring conference ideas are similarity, information, and human-in-the-loop learning. Similarity decides which names may describe the same relation. Information is saved by removing redundant labels without losing semantic coverage. Human review keeps the automated comparison from turning near matches into wrong merges.
ww: The approach should improve over the naive alternatives because each part handles the failure mode it is suited for. Exact string rules cannot see meaning, but a language model can compare differently worded property names and descriptions at the level of intended relation. That makes it useful for finding synonymy, where the same idea is hidden under several labels. Pure automation would be risky because ontology work is full of borderline cases: a small wording difference may reflect a real scientific distinction, not just naming noise. Human engineering supplies that judgment and also enforces the discipline of a shared schema. The result works if most redundancy is linguistic and structural rather than deeply domain-specific in a way the model cannot detect. Consolidation also helps downstream tools for a simple reason: when one relationship has one preferred name, search, comparison, and graph traversal no longer need to guess which duplicate property to follow. Cleaner predicates make each triple easier for machines to interpret.
po: The payoff is a more usable ORKG property ontology. According to the abstract, OPO-Consolidated improves schema conciseness by resolving synonymy and redundancy, and improves semantic consistency by enforcing uniform naming conventions. In practical terms, that means fewer duplicate relation names, clearer meanings for software, and a stronger basis for scientific knowledge graphs used in retrieval-augmented generation. The work also offers a migration path implied by consolidation rather than replacement: the value is not inventing a separate knowledge base, but cleaning the vocabulary that existing ORKG data depends on.
limits: Several assumptions have to hold. The existing property names and available descriptions must contain enough language signal for the model and engineers to judge when meanings overlap. Human reviewers must be qualified and consistent, because their decisions define the final ontology quality. The abstract reports evaluation on a gold standard dataset of 153 research papers, but it does not prove that every scientific field, property edge case, or future contributor behavior is covered. It also shows improved conciseness and naming consistency, not a direct end-to-end proof that every downstream retrieval-augmented answer becomes more correct.
